He argues that the hearing officer aired in finding that the installation of the front and rear entry gates, the pool removal, and the roof replacement were necessary repairs. He further argued that he should have received a higher decrease and a longer period of reduction for noise, dust, trip and fall hazards, and lack of communication. The board reviews this matter as an appelllet body. Therefore, it should affirm the hearing officer's findings if they're supported by substantial evidence under the board's construction decrease regulations. Decreases may be granted for substantial impact only if the construction is for work that does not constitute necessary repairs or maintenance. For work that is a necessary repair, decreases may only be granted for unavoidable impacts if the work is carried out in an unreasonable manner or takes an unreasonably long time to complete. And as petitioner, tenants bear the evidentiary burden of proving their claims by a prepoundonderance of the evidence. Here, the hearing officer found that the installation of the front and rear entry doors, the removal of the pool, and the roof replacement were all necessary repairs. Therefore, decreases could only be granted if the work was done in an unreasonable manner or took an unreasonably long time. Mr. Detliffson argues to the contrary, but as detailed in the staff report, substantial evidence supports the hearing officer's findings that these projects were necessary repairs and that Mr. Mr. Detliffson failed to meet his evidentiary burden of proving otherwise. Mr. Detliffson also argued that he should have received higher decreases for those conditions for which he was granted a decrease. In determining the amount of a decrease, the percentage reduction must be supported by substantial evidence and be in accordance with the range set forth in the board's regulations. It must also reflect the severity of the impact as established by the evidence in the record and must also be proportionate to the totality of the housing services provided by the rent. And in doing so must take into consideration any other percentage reductions for the same period because you might wind up having more than 100% rent reduction, for example, and that wouldn't be correct. As detailed in the staff report, substantial evidence supports the amount of the decreases granted and they are in accordance with the range set forth in the board's regulations. Finally, as also detailed in the staff report, the record reasonably supports the denial of decreases for noise from the roof replacement, dust on car from paint, and safety impacts from the gates being left open because Mr. Detliffson failed to meet his evidentiary burden approving these claims by a proponents of the evidence.
